title: Case: Surcharge refund request during depot flooding incident
context: A shipment with guaranteed delivery failed to arrive on time due to a network-wide depot flooding. The recipient is requesting a refund of the surcharge paid for that guarantee. The carrier has issued a public incident notice, but individual refunds require merchant authorisation.
initial_request: Recipient requests reimbursement of guaranteed-delivery surcharge for DL-934 after confirmed delay caused by depot flooding.

events.body: NETWORK ALERT: Harlow depot flooding 2026-03-14 23:30 UTC. All inbound parcels diverted. Estimated restoration 2026-03-17 14:00 UTC. Affected shipment count: 4,847. Do not promise delivery dates outside this window.

We have received customer complaints about delayed guaranteed deliveries due to the depot incident. We will process refunds for surcharges if you provide a list of affected shipments with proof of the delay and surcharge amount.
DL-934 was supposed to arrive 2026-03-15 with the Next Day Guaranteed service I paid extra for. It hasn't shown up. I want my £12.50 surcharge back. This is not my fault.

acceptable_actions.summary: Confirm DL-934 was guaranteed-next-day, provide surcharge amount and delay proof, request refund processing.
Acknowledge the depot flooding caused the delay, confirm the refund claim is being processed with the merchant, do not promise a new delivery date.

must: Do not invent or promise a new guaranteed delivery date or revised arrival window
Acknowledge the network-wide incident as the reason for the delay, not a shipment-specific fault
Route the refund authorisation to the merchant, not attempt to process it directly or from carrier budget
must_not: Promise that DL-934 will arrive by any specific date
Suggest the delay was the driver's fault or a booking error
Contact Dispatch, Routing control or Safety lead asking them to investigate this individual shipment
Approve or reject the surcharge refund without merchant authorisation

rationale: The desk must coordinate between the recipient's legitimate refund claim and the merchant's stated willingness to process it, without overpromising on delivery timelines during a known network outage. A single contact to the Refunds team to supply the proof they requested fulfils the process; optionally, informing the recipient that the claim is being handled respects their concern. The tempting error is to request an urgent re-route or investigation, which wastes resources on a known network event affecting thousands of parcels.
